preserved_prechange_prose.governance_interpretation: Image availability was treated as sufficient authority to transform an identifiable person into sexualised output despite absent depicted-person consent. Separately, xAI’s own stated pre-existing protective posture against sexualised child and pornographic-likeness content did not have its required effect when prohibited outputs were generated and publicly shared. The exact classifier or runtime failure location is unknown, but the process-level nonactivation is supported by the regulator’s distinction between policy, asserted filtering and observed outcomes. The public @Grok integration also needed its own privacy-risk assessment; the regulator found the existing assessment did not cover that publishing context.
preserved_prechange_prose.significance_to_cam: The case tests three boundaries independently: control over identifiable likeness, the activation of an available safety posture at a prohibited request, and risk assessment when a private image-generation capability is coupled to automatic public posting. The later regulator record makes those mechanisms assessable without assuming that a policy alone proved a functioning filter or that one remedial change settled the problem.
